items.title: L14: Designing a presentation as an argument for senior panels
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles: Communicating and Influencing; Seeing the Big Picture (GOV.UK)
items.body:
At SEO level, presentation exercises usually test whether you can shape a view, not just report information. The panel often plays senior stakeholders with limited time and strong opinions, and it will judge your command of the subject, your sense of priorities and your ability to hold the room.

A reliable design starts from the audience. Ask what they already believe, what they need to decide and what they are likely to worry about. Then fix your core message: the one thing you want remembered. Everything else serves it.

The argument usually runs in three parts. The case for change explains why the status quo is not good enough, using evidence rather than assertion. The proposal sets out what you would do, how it would work and what it would cost. The delivery section covers risks, dependencies and how success would be measured. Weak presentations spend most of the time on the first part, which the audience often already accepts.

Senior audiences value judgement about what matters. Say what you are deliberately leaving out and why. Show you have considered the strongest alternative and explain why you do not recommend it. Give a view on the greatest risk and what you would do if it materialised.

Practise the opening and closing until they are fluent, because these are what the panel remembers. In between, rely on a few clear points rather than a script. Use pauses. Give the audience time to absorb a figure or a claim before you move on.

In questions, treat each as a chance to reinforce your message. If you are challenged on a fact you cannot verify, say what you know, what you would need to check and when you could report back. Credibility depends on honesty about the edge of your knowledge.

questions.prompt: In designing a presentation for a senior panel, what should you establish before choosing content?

options.text: Which of your own achievements will make the strongest impression on the panel, so you can feature them
Which slide template the department uses for senior presentations, so that the format meets expectations
How many slides the previous successful candidate used in the same exercise, so you can match them
What the audience already believes, what they need to decide and what worries them

questions.hint: Audience analysis decides what the content must do.

questions.prompt: A candidate gives 70 per cent of the time to why the current approach is failing, a point the panel already accepts. What is the main fault?

options.text: The case for change should be left out of a senior presentation altogether
Presentations at this level should concentrate on risks and ignore the existing position
The candidate should have spoken more slowly to make the case more forcefully
Too little time is left for the proposal and its delivery, which the panel must judge

questions.hint: Time should follow what the audience needs to decide.

questions.prompt: Which element completes the three-part argument of a strong presentation, after the case for change and the proposal?

options.text: An appendix of background papers for the panel to read afterwards
Delivery: risks, dependencies and how success would be measured
A list of the other options that were rejected, in order of cost
A summary of the career experience that qualifies you to make the proposal

questions.hint: Senior panels want to see how an idea would be carried out and tested.

questions.prompt: Why does saying what you have deliberately left out help at senior level?

options.text: It ensures the panel cannot criticise you for missing information, since you have named the gaps
It gives you a reason to cut the presentation short if you run out of time before the end
It lets you avoid questions on topics that you have not prepared, as the panel has been warned
It shows judgement about priorities and makes clear that the omission was a choice

questions.hint: Senior roles are about deciding what matters.

questions.prompt: Why is it useful to address the strongest alternative to your recommendation?

options.text: It shows you have tested your own view and gives a reason to prefer your option
It makes your own option look stronger by comparison with a weak rival that you can easily dismiss
It gives the panel a different option to approve if they disagree with yours, which keeps the session positive
It reduces the time available for questions that might challenge the main points of your proposal

questions.hint: Engaging with the best counter-argument builds credibility.

questions.prompt: Which parts of a presentation should you rehearse most thoroughly?

options.text: The opening and closing, because they are what a panel remembers
The slides, because the panel will follow them closely and any error in them will be noticed
The middle section, because it contains most of the evidence and the panel will test it hardest
The transitions between sections, because that is where candidates most often lose their place

questions.hint: A fluent start and finish frame the whole message.

questions.prompt: A panellist asks about a statistic that you cannot verify. Which answer is strongest?

options.text: What I know is the trend; I would need to check the exact figure and can report back tomorrow
I believe the figure is correct, as it came from a source that is generally considered reliable
I will give you an estimate now and correct it later if it turns out to be wrong in any way
The figure is not central to my argument, so I would rather not spend time on it in this session

questions.hint: Honesty about the limit of knowledge, with a plan to check, protects credibility.

questions.prompt: Why use pauses in a presentation?

options.text: They fill time when you have prepared too little material
They signal to the panel that questions are welcome at that point
They allow you to check your notes without the audience noticing
They let the audience absorb a figure or claim before you move on

questions.hint: Pauses give weight to key points and help listeners.

questions.prompt: How should you treat questions after the presentation?

options.text: As a separate exercise unrelated to the presentation
As prompts for additional detail you did not have time to cover
As chances to reinforce your core message with evidence
As threats to be closed down as quickly as possible

questions.hint: Good answers return to the message and strengthen it.

questions.prompt: Which statement describes a core message correctly?

options.text: The conclusion on the final slide, repeated word for word so that the panel can note it down
The title of the presentation as it appears on the first slide, which frames the whole talk
A summary of the content of each of your slides in turn, delivered at the end of the session
The one thing you want remembered, to which everything else contributes

questions.hint: A single message focuses the argument.

items.title: L14: Written exercises: submissions, briefings and lines to take
items.source: Civil Service Jobs candidate guidance and Civil Service Code (GOV.UK)
items.body:
Senior written exercises often use the main Civil Service document types. A submission asks a decision-maker to choose or approve something and recommends an option. A briefing prepares someone for a meeting or event, setting out what they need to know, who will attend, what the other side wants and what to say. Lines to take are short, agreed statements that someone can use when asked about a subject, often in a media or parliamentary setting. Each has a different reader and purpose, and exercises sometimes combine them, so read the task carefully and decide which you are writing.

A good briefing opens with the purpose of the meeting and what the reader should aim to achieve. It then gives the essential background in a few lines, the positions of those involved, the likely difficult questions with suggested answers, and any sensitivities. It must be short enough to read in the minutes before the event.

Lines to take should be accurate, brief and consistent with existing government policy. They should not speculate, make promises the department cannot keep or go beyond what has been agreed. If a question is outside the agreed position, the lines should say so and suggest a holding response.

All three depend on accuracy and impartiality. The Civil Service Code requires officials to provide information and advice honestly and objectively, and not to mislead. An exercise may include a trap, such as a statistic that has been revised or a request for wording that overstates the evidence. The right response is to use the correct figure and flag the issue, not to quietly choose the more helpful version.

Check the final version for tone, accuracy and fit with the reader. Ask what a busy, senior person would do with the document in the next five minutes, and whether it helps them.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of a briefing?

options.text: To ask a decision-maker to choose between options, with a recommendation and the reasons for it
To prepare someone for a meeting or event with what they need to know and say
To record what was agreed at a meeting after it has taken place, with actions and owners
To provide an agreed statement for use when asked about a subject, without any further background

questions.hint: A briefing prepares the reader for an occasion.

questions.prompt: What are lines to take?

options.text: Short, agreed statements that someone can use when asked about a subject
A list of questions that a minister expects to be asked in Parliament, with the answers drafted
Guidance on how an official should behave when speaking to the media on behalf of a department
Detailed minutes of the discussions that led to a decision, circulated for the record afterwards

questions.hint: They give consistent wording on a subject.

questions.prompt: Which opening best suits a briefing for a director before a meeting with a supplier?

options.text: A history of the contract since it was awarded, so that the director knows how the relationship developed
The purpose of the meeting and what you should aim to achieve from it
A list of the supplier's recent press coverage, so that the director is aware of its reputation
A summary of the department's policy on procurement, so that the director knows the rules that apply

questions.hint: A briefing begins with purpose and desired outcome.

questions.prompt: A question outside the agreed position is likely. What should the lines to take do?

options.text: Offer a plausible answer based on the department's general approach, so that the speaker is not caught out
Suggest that the speaker gives their own view if they feel able to, since they know the subject
Say that it is outside the agreed position and suggest a holding response
Leave the question out so that the lines stay short and the speaker is not distracted by it

questions.hint: Officials must not go beyond what has been agreed.

questions.prompt: Why should lines to take avoid speculation and promises?

options.text: Speculation is only allowed in written submissions, where there is room to set out the reasoning
They must be accurate and consistent with agreed policy and not commit the department further
They need to be as short as possible so that anyone can remember them without needing notes
Promises can only be made by a person of a certain grade, so lines for others should avoid them

questions.hint: Lines have to reflect the agreed position.

questions.prompt: The exercise asks you to include a statistic that has since been revised downwards. What should you do?

options.text: Leave out the statistic and refer only to the trend
Use the revised figure and flag the change to the reader
Use the original figure because the task asked for it
Use the higher figure and add a footnote about the revision

questions.hint: The Code requires honest, accurate information.

questions.prompt: A senior colleague asks for wording that slightly overstates the evidence. What should an official do?

options.text: Use the wording but add a caveat in the covering note, so that the record shows your concern
Explain the concern and offer accurate wording that still supports the message
Refuse to draft the document until the instruction is withdrawn, so that you are not part of it
Use the wording, since a senior colleague has asked for it and takes responsibility for the message

questions.hint: Honest advice and a constructive alternative.

questions.prompt: Which Civil Service Code value most directly applies when you are asked to present evidence in a more favourable light than is accurate?

options.text: Integrity in the use of resources
Loyalty to ministers
Honesty
Impartiality

questions.prompt: A document will be read in the five minutes before an event. What should you ask yourself?

options.text: Whether every point has been given a reference
Whether the document shows how much work was done
What the reader will do with it and whether it helps
Whether the document is as long as other documents of this kind

questions.prompt: In an exercise that combines a submission and lines to take, what is the best approach?

options.text: Identify the reader and purpose of each document and write each accordingly
Ask the panel which document to prioritise, since time is too short to write both properly
Write one document and add a short summary for the other, so that the work is not duplicated
Write the lines to take first and use them as the submission, since they hold the agreed position

items.title: L14: Panels testing judgement under ambiguity
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles: Making Effective Decisions; Seeing the Big Picture (GOV.UK)
items.body:
At SEO level, many questions have no clean answer. The panel gives you a situation with incomplete information, competing priorities or a risk of harm either way, and watches how you reason. These scenarios test Making Effective Decisions and Seeing the Big Picture, and they are scored on the quality of your thinking more than on the choice you reach.

A helpful method is to separate four steps. First, define the decision: what exactly has to be decided, by whom and by when? Second, identify what you know, what you do not and what you could find out quickly. Third, weigh the options against the objectives and the principles that apply, such as legality, fairness, value for money and the public interest. Fourth, decide, state your reasons and say how you would check and adjust.

Stating assumptions aloud is important. 'If the data is accurate, I would do X; if it is not, I would do Y' shows you understand the sensitivity of your decision. Equally important is naming what you would do first to reduce uncertainty, such as a short call to an expert, as long as the situation allows time.

Panels may deliberately add information as you answer: 'The minister's office has now asked for an answer by noon.' Adapt without abandoning your reasoning. Say how the new fact changes the options and whether your priorities change. A candidate who abandons the analysis in response to pressure appears unsteady; one who ignores new information appears rigid.

Do not hide behind 'it depends'. After setting out what it depends on, commit to the best course and explain it.

Where a decision carries ethical or legal issues, name them and say whom you would consult. Knowing the limits of your authority is part of good judgement.

questions.prompt: Which sequence best describes a sound approach to an ambiguous scenario?

options.text: Ask the panel for more information until the position is clear, then decide when nothing is left unknown
List every option you can think of, choose the one that sounds best and then work out how to justify it
Define the decision, identify what is known and unknown, weigh options against objectives and principles, then decide and say how you would check
Decide quickly to show decisiveness and then adjust your decision as new facts emerge during the discussion

questions.hint: It structures thinking and shows reasoning.

questions.prompt: Why state your assumptions aloud?

options.text: It saves time by avoiding the need for further analysis once the assumptions have been accepted
It shows you understand how sensitive the decision is to what you do not know
It gives you an excuse if the decision proves to be wrong, because the assumptions were made explicit
It allows the panel to decide whether the answer is correct before you move on to the next point

questions.prompt: The panel adds a new fact midway through your answer. What is the best response?

options.text: Restart your analysis from the beginning
Say how the fact changes the options and adapt your reasoning
Ask the panel to confirm that the fact is correct before using it
Stay with your original answer, since the new fact is not part of the question

questions.prompt: Which candidate behaviour suggests rigidity?

options.text: Revising the analysis when the facts change, so that the final answer reflects the new position
Ignoring new information that changes the options
Pausing for a few seconds before answering a difficult question put by the panel
Asking a clarifying question before answering, even when the scenario seems clear enough

questions.prompt: Which candidate behaviour suggests instability under pressure?

options.text: Naming the principle that applies and explaining how it shapes the decision you reach
Saying how you would check the result of the decision and adjust it if the position changed
Abandoning the analysis as soon as a deadline is mentioned
Setting out what you would do first to reduce the uncertainty in the situation

questions.prompt: Why is 'it depends' a weak ending to an answer?

options.text: It is not allowed in the interview rules, which require every candidate to give a direct answer
The panel needs a decision and reasons, after you have set out what it depends on
It takes too long to explain, and the panel has other candidates to see in the time available
It suggests that you do not know the subject well enough to commit to a specific course of action

questions.prompt: A scenario has a possible legal issue. What should you do?

options.text: Ignore the issue unless the panel raises it, since legal analysis is not part of the exercise
Say that legal matters are always for the minister to decide, so that nothing is done by officials
Make a decision on the legal point yourself as the senior official present, so the matter is closed
Name the issue, say whom you would consult and show you understand the limit of your authority

questions.prompt: What does 'Seeing the Big Picture' add to an ambiguous scenario?

options.text: A preference for long-term over short-term benefits in every case, whatever the cost at the time
A detailed knowledge of every department's policy, so that your decision can be coordinated with theirs
A focus on the decisions of the most senior stakeholder, as their view shapes the wider objectives
Awareness of how your decision fits with wider objectives and public interest

questions.prompt: What is a sound first step to reduce uncertainty if the situation allows time?

options.text: A decision by the most senior person present, who can accept the uncertainty on behalf of the group
A full review of all of the relevant papers before any action is taken, so that nothing is missed
A short, targeted check, such as a call to an expert or a data owner
A request for a delay until all of the information is available, so that the decision is well founded

questions.prompt: How are scenario answers usually scored?

options.text: On the quality of your reasoning more than the specific decision you reach
On whether you match the decision that the panel had in mind when it wrote the scenario
On how quickly you give an answer, since a delay suggests you are unsure of the right course
On the number of options that you list, since a wider range shows broader thinking

items.title: L14: Strengths, Behaviours and the overdone strength at senior level
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles: Strengths and Behaviours (GOV.UK)
items.body:
At senior grades, strengths questions are often more searching. Panels want to know how you lead when under pressure, what you do when your preferred approach does not work and how well you know yourself. A candidate who describes only positive qualities can seem unreflective.

A strength used without judgement can become a weakness. A drive for results may turn into impatience with those who work more slowly. A love of detail may delay decisions. A wish to help may make delegation hard. These are sometimes called overdone strengths. Showing that you recognise yours, and how you manage them, signals maturity: 'I like to get things done quickly, which can leave others behind, so I now check in with the team before moving to the next phase.'

Panels also look for consistency across the interview. If your strengths answers show you prefer to work alone but your Behaviour examples describe building teams, the panel may wonder which is real. Reflect before the interview on how your strengths show up in the examples you intend to use.

Strengths questions may also test how you cope when you are asked to work in an area you do not enjoy. The honest answer acknowledges that it takes more effort and describes how you manage it, such as arranging tasks at times of high energy or drawing on a colleague's complementary strength. This shows you can deliver outside your comfort zone.

When asked about energy and motivation, link them to the work of the role. A genuine enthusiasm for solving difficult problems for the public will be heard differently from a general wish for responsibility.

Finally, avoid performing. Panels are used to hearing rehearsed phrases about passion and teamwork. Specific, personal and honest answers stand out.

questions.prompt: What is an overdone strength?

options.text: A strength that is claimed without any evidence, which a panel is unlikely to accept
A strength used without judgement so that it becomes a weakness
A strength that is shared by most of the other candidates, so it does not set you apart
A strength that is relevant to a different role from the one that is being applied for

questions.hint: It describes strengths that go too far.

questions.prompt: Which example is an overdone strength?

options.text: A high standard in written work that other colleagues admire and often ask you to review
A strong preference for working with colleagues who are on the same grade as you are
A drive for results that becomes impatience with colleagues who work more slowly
A habit of arriving early for meetings and preparing for them carefully in advance

questions.hint: It shows a strength turning counterproductive.

questions.prompt: Which answer best shows self-awareness about a strength?

options.text: I have no real downsides, because I plan carefully and so avoid the problems that others meet
I get things done quickly, which is why my teams always deliver on time and to a good standard
I like to get things done quickly, which can leave others behind, so I now check in with the team before the next phase
I am sometimes told that I move quickly, but I think that is a good thing in a busy department

questions.hint: It names the downside and the control.

questions.prompt: A candidate's strengths answers say they prefer to work alone, but their Behaviour examples describe building teams. What is the effect?

options.text: The panel will see this as evidence of versatility
The panel will ignore the strengths answers
The panel may doubt which account is real
The panel will score the Behaviours higher because they are better evidenced

questions.prompt: How should you answer a question about working in an area you do not enjoy?

options.text: Say that you are happy to do any work that is required, and that you never find tasks a problem
Say that you have never found any work difficult, since you adapt quickly to what is needed
Say that you would avoid such work where possible and focus on the areas where you perform best
Acknowledge it takes more effort and explain how you manage it

questions.prompt: Which approach shows that you can deliver outside your comfort zone?

options.text: Delegating the task to someone who enjoys it, so that the work is done by the person best suited
Asking your manager to reallocate it permanently so that you can focus on other responsibilities
Arranging difficult tasks for times of high energy or drawing on a colleague's complementary strength
Doing the task at the end of the day, when pressure from other work has eased

questions.prompt: When asked about motivation, what makes an answer more convincing?

options.text: Describing what you enjoy about your current team, which shows how well you work with others
Naming the values of the Civil Service, which shows that you understand the organisation
Describing your ambition to reach a more senior grade, since the panel wants to see drive
Linking it to the work of the role and the public it serves

questions.prompt: Why might panels distrust rehearsed phrases about passion and teamwork?

options.text: They are common and tell the panel nothing specific about you
They are not allowed in strengths interviews, where every answer must be spontaneous
They suggest that you do not understand the role, because genuine enthusiasm is more concrete
They always take too long to deliver, which reduces the time available for later questions

questions.prompt: How can you prepare for the consistency check between strengths and Behaviours?

options.text: Reflect on how your strengths show up in the examples you will use
Write down answers to every possible strengths question, so that you can deliver them smoothly
Ask a colleague to review your strengths, and prepare only the ones that they agree with
Choose examples that avoid mentioning your strengths, so that the two cannot be compared

questions.prompt: Which question is a strengths question?

options.text: What do you do when your preferred approach does not work?
Tell us how you managed a budget over the last year and what you did when it came under pressure
Describe a time when you led a team through change and what you learned from it
Give an example of an important decision you took and explain how you reached it

items.title: L14: Leading through other managers
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles: Leadership; Developing Self and Others (GOV.UK)
items.body:
At SEO level, you often lead managers as well as individual staff. This changes the evidence panels expect. Leading a team directly means setting tasks and giving feedback. Leading managers means setting direction and standards, then trusting them to run their teams while holding them to account.

Four behaviours matter. First, clarity of expectations: managers need to know what outcomes you want, how much freedom they have and where they must come to you. Second, delegation with accountability: you give real decisions to others, but you remain answerable for the result. Third, support and challenge: regular one-to-ones, honest feedback and help to develop their own leadership. Fourth, consistency: managers who see standards applied unevenly will apply them unevenly in turn.

A common failure is micromanaging, or its opposite, abdicating. A leader who checks every detail takes the decisions away from managers and slows the team; one who leaves them without guidance risks drift. Effective leaders watch outcomes and trends, step in when measures slip and explain why they are doing so.

When a manager in your area is underperforming, you need to address both the manager and the effect on their team. Coaching comes first, then clear expectations, then a formal route if needed. You also protect the team, for example by reassigning work or giving them a route to raise concerns.

In interviews, expect probes on how you know your managers are performing, what you do when a team is struggling and how you develop future leaders. Good answers use specific measures, such as engagement results, delivery against plan and promotion of people you have developed, and give examples of conversations with managers.

Be honest about what you do not see. Leading at a distance requires deliberate ways of finding out, such as skip-level conversations and visiting teams.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes leading managers from leading individual staff?

options.text: Giving tasks to each team member directly and checking progress at regular intervals
Visiting teams less often than the managers do, so that the managers keep their own authority
Setting direction and standards and holding managers to account while they run their teams
Taking decisions on behalf of managers when they are busy, so that delivery does not slow

questions.hint: It is leadership at one remove.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes delegation with accountability?

options.text: You give decisions to others and are no longer responsible for what happens as a result
You keep the decisions but ask others to do the work and report back to you each week
You review each decision before it is acted on so that errors do not reach the team
You give real decisions to others but remain answerable for the outcome

questions.prompt: A leader checks every detail of their managers' work. What is the likely effect?

options.text: It shows managers that the leader values accuracy and the standards that the department expects
It prevents errors being repeated, as the leader sees every mistake and can correct it at once
It takes decisions away from managers and slows the team
It improves quality across the team, because every piece of work is checked by a senior person

questions.prompt: What is the risk of abdicating?

options.text: Managers become over-reliant on the leader, who is then asked to settle every difficult question
Teams drift without guidance and standards slip
Managers take too many decisions on their own, which the leader then has to reverse
Teams begin to compete with one another, since nobody is coordinating the priorities

questions.prompt: How should a leader find out whether managers are performing?

options.text: Observe each team daily, so that the leader sees how the work is done at first hand
Ask each manager to rate their own performance, and review the ratings once a year
Look at outcomes and trends and have regular honest conversations
Wait for managers to raise problems, as they know their teams and will say if help is needed

questions.prompt: A manager in your area is underperforming. Which order of steps is best?

options.text: Waiting a year to see whether performance improves, so that the manager has a fair chance
A change of manager at once, to avoid any delay in improving the position for the team
Coaching, then clear expectations, then a formal route if needed, while protecting the team
A formal process first, to set the standard clearly and make the consequences plain to the manager

questions.prompt: Why is consistency important when leading managers?

options.text: Consistency makes decisions faster, because managers do not need to ask the leader for guidance
It reduces the number of conversations needed, because standards are then understood by all
Managers apply standards as unevenly as they see them applied
Managers prefer clear rules and will follow whichever rule the leader announces first

questions.prompt: Which measure best supports a claim that you develop future leaders?

options.text: Positive feedback from your own manager about how you lead your area
The number of training courses you have attended on leadership and development
The size of the team that you lead and the budget that you manage
Promotions and development progress of people you have supported, with specific examples

questions.prompt: How can a leader at a distance find out what is really happening?

options.text: By reading the monthly management reports, which show how each team is performing
By commissioning an annual survey of staff, which gives the most reliable picture
By asking managers to report problems as they arise, so that nothing is hidden
Through skip-level conversations and visits to teams

questions.prompt: Which question might a panel use to probe leadership of managers?

options.text: How do you know your managers are performing, and what do you do when they are not?
Which of your teams do you enjoy leading most, and what makes it different?
How many people report to you, and how many of them are themselves managers?
What is your management style, and how do your teams respond to it?

questions.hint: It asks for evidence and action.

items.title: L14: Leading in ambiguity: setting direction and priorities
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles: Seeing the Big Picture; Leadership (GOV.UK)
items.body:
Senior roles require you to give direction when the future is uncertain. The panel will ask how you set priorities, communicate the 'why' and keep people focused when plans change. Good answers show structure and humility.

Setting direction begins with understanding the purpose of the organisation and the outcomes it must deliver. From this you can set a small number of priorities. A team told that everything is a priority will not know where to put its effort. Say which priorities rank first, what you will stop doing, and how you will review the ranking.

Communicating the reason matters as much as the content. People can accept hard decisions better when they understand the thinking and see that their concerns were heard. A direction that is explained once and then never mentioned again is easily forgotten, so effective leaders repeat key messages in different forms and check understanding.

When the situation is uncertain, set direction in stages. Define what is clear, what is likely and what is unknown. Make decisions that can be reversed quickly where information is poor, and invest more heavily only when evidence builds. Tell the team that the plan will be reviewed at set points, so that change is expected rather than a surprise.

Good leaders also stay open to challenge. They ask the team where the plan might fail and welcome dissent before decisions are made. After the decision, they expect support.

In interviews, give examples showing how you set direction, what trade-offs you made and how you handled a change of course. Describe how you told the team and how you maintained trust. An answer that shows no change of mind can seem rigid, while one that shows a change made for good reasons shows judgement.

questions.prompt: Why is a team told that everything is a priority likely to struggle?

options.text: It will rely on the manager to decide each day
It will compete with other teams
It will work more quickly to meet every demand
It will not know where to place its effort

questions.prompt: Which statement best demonstrates prioritisation?

options.text: These two outcomes come first, we will stop this piece of work and we will review the ranking in three months
We will concentrate on the work that is most visible to senior managers, as it carries the most risk
We will deliver whatever is asked for by the most senior person, in the order that requests arrive
All of the work is important and we will do as much of it as we can in the time available

questions.hint: It names priorities, a stop and a review.

questions.prompt: Why should leaders repeat their key messages?

options.text: A direction explained once is easily forgotten, and repetition helps to check understanding
Repeating key messages is part of the Civil Service Code and its requirements on communication
Teams are more likely to follow a message that is repeated by the leader, whatever its content
Repetition ensures consistency between leaders in different parts of the department

questions.prompt: How does a leader set direction when the future is uncertain?

options.text: In stages, separating what is clear, what is likely and what is unknown
By waiting until the position is certain, so that the direction does not need to change
By choosing the most likely scenario and planning for it in full, whatever the other possibilities
By delegating the decision to the team, who are closest to the work and can adapt to change

questions.prompt: Which decision is suited to uncertain conditions?

options.text: One that can be reversed quickly if the evidence changes
A decision taken by the team without the leader, so that the leader can respond to later change
A decision postponed until all of the facts are known, so that there is no risk of error
A long-term contract that locks in the current approach, so that the team has stability

questions.prompt: Why tell the team that the plan will be reviewed at set points?

options.text: So that change is expected rather than a surprise
So that the plan can be altered at any time by anyone who thinks that it is not working
So that the leader is not blamed if the plan changes, since the review points were agreed
So that the team has less need for direction between reviews, as the plan is fixed until then

questions.prompt: What is the benefit of asking the team where the plan might fail?

options.text: It reduces the need for the leader to analyse the risks, as the team will have done it
It surfaces risks and builds ownership before decisions are made
It shows the leader does not know the answer, which encourages the team to take over
It gives the team a chance to change the decision, as their view is final on matters of detail

questions.prompt: How should a leader behave after a decision is made following consultation?

options.text: Delegate responsibility for the decision to the team, who will then see that it is carried out
Expect support, while remaining open to evidence that it is not working
Revisit the decision whenever someone disagrees, so that nobody feels that they have not been heard
Stop listening to challenge, since the consultation has finished and the decision is now final

questions.prompt: Why can an answer that shows no change of mind seem weak?

options.text: It shows too much confidence, which a panel treats as a warning sign in a senior leader
It lacks a clear plan, because a plan that never changed was probably not specific enough
It can suggest rigidity or that the leader did not respond to new evidence
It does not describe a result, so the panel cannot judge the effect of the decision

questions.hint: Change for good reasons shows judgement.

questions.prompt: Which element should be included when describing how you handled a change of course?

options.text: The date of the change and the date on which the new plan took effect
How you told the team and how you maintained trust
The cost of the change and the budget from which it was funded
The name of the senior person who agreed it and the reasons they gave

items.title: L14: Managing upwards and disagreeing with senior people
items.source: Civil Service Code; Civil Service Success Profiles: Communicating and Influencing (GOV.UK)
items.body:
Senior civil servants are expected to give honest advice to those above them, including ministers, and to carry out lawful decisions once taken. Panels often ask about moments when you had to push back on a senior person, because the way you do so shows judgement, courage and respect.

A constructive approach has several parts. Prepare your case: be clear about the issue, the evidence and the consequences. Choose your moment and your setting, usually privately and early, so that the person has time to reflect and is not embarrassed. State your concern as a concern about the outcome, not about the person: 'I am worried that this timetable puts the quality of the service at risk' is more effective than 'You are being unrealistic'. Offer a way forward, such as an alternative timetable or a phased approach. Listen to the reply, as the person may hold information you do not. If they decide against your advice, and the decision is lawful, you carry it out and, where appropriate, record your advice.

Some concerns are different. If you are asked to act in a way that is illegal, that constitutes misconduct or that is a serious breach of the Civil Service Code, you should raise it first with your line manager or a senior official, and, if necessary, use the department's nominated officers and the route to the Civil Service Commission. The Code protects those who raise concerns in good faith.

Managing upwards also means making a senior person's job easier. Keep them informed of problems early, bring solutions with problems, and learn how they prefer to receive information. No surprises is a useful rule.

In answers, avoid presenting senior people as obstacles or villains. Show respect, tenacity and a willingness to commit once a decision has been made.

questions.prompt: Which wording best expresses a concern to a senior person?

options.text: You are being unrealistic about the timetable, and I think that it needs to be looked at again
The timetable is not something that I can support, and I would like you to change it
I am worried that this timetable puts the quality of the service at risk
I think you have misjudged the timetable, and the evidence suggests that you did so before

questions.hint: It focuses on outcomes, not the person.

questions.prompt: When is it usually best to raise a concern with a senior person?

options.text: In a team meeting, so that the issue is seen by all and the senior person is held to account
Just before the decision is due, so that the evidence is fresh and the reasons are clear
After the decision, in writing, so that the record shows what you advised at that point
Early and in private, so that they have time to think and are not embarrassed

questions.prompt: Why should you offer a way forward when raising a concern?

options.text: It shows that you are as senior as the person you are challenging, which supports your case
It makes it harder for the senior person to refuse, because the alternative is already prepared
It makes the conversation constructive and shows you have thought about solutions
It reduces the need for evidence, as the proposal speaks for itself and can be tested later

questions.prompt: A senior official decides against your advice in a lawful decision. What should you do?

options.text: Delay implementation until the evidence changes, so that the decision can be reviewed in time
Carry it out and, where appropriate, record your advice
Continue to argue until they reverse the decision, since the Code requires you to give honest advice
Ask a more senior person to overrule it, so that the proper outcome is reached for the department

questions.hint: Officials advise and carry out lawful decisions.

questions.prompt: What should you do if asked to act illegally?

options.text: Carry out the request and record your objection, so that the responsibility lies with the person who asked
Report it to the media so that the public is protected before the action is taken
Refuse to speak to the person who made the request until the department has taken advice
Raise it with your line manager or senior official, and if necessary use nominated officers and the Civil Service Commission route

questions.prompt: Which phrase describes a good principle for managing upwards?

options.text: Wait until you have a perfect solution before raising issues, so that you do not worry the senior person
Avoid surprises: tell senior people of problems early and bring options
Avoid raising problems that may reflect badly on you until you are sure that they cannot be solved
Keep information to yourself until it is asked for, so that senior people are not overloaded

questions.prompt: Why listen to the reply when you challenge a senior person?

options.text: It allows the conversation to end sooner
It gives you time to prepare the next argument
It shows that you accept their authority
They may hold information you do not have

questions.prompt: How should you describe a senior person in an interview about disagreement?

options.text: As an obstacle that had to be overcome, since that shows how determined you were
With respect, focusing on the issue and not on the person
In terms that make clear they were wrong, since the panel must see why you disagreed
Without naming them or their role, so that the account is not seen as critical

questions.prompt: What does the Civil Service Code provide for officials who raise concerns in good faith?

options.text: A right to leave the department with full pay if the concern is not resolved
An exemption from carrying out lawful decisions where they conflict with the official's own view
Protection and a route to raise concerns, including to the Civil Service Commission
A guarantee of promotion for anyone who raises a concern that is later upheld

questions.prompt: Which behaviour shows tenacity without disrespect?

options.text: Raising the concern in front of the whole team so that the issue is understood by all
Raising the concern again with new evidence if the situation changes
Copying in senior colleagues to apply pressure, so that the decision is taken at the right level
Sending repeated emails until the person responds, so that the concern is not ignored

items.title: L14: Proving personal contribution in large-scale achievements
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles: Behaviours; Government Functional Standards (GOV.UK)
items.body:
Senior interview examples often involve outcomes achieved by large groups over long periods. Panels still need to know what you personally contributed. Three techniques help.

The first is to identify the decisions that would not have been taken in the same way without you. These might include a change of direction, a risk you flagged that others missed, a negotiation that unlocked agreement, or an appointment you made. Describe the situation at the time, the alternatives, your choice and the effect.

The second is to set out the counterfactual honestly. Ask yourself what would have happened without your contribution, and give a measured answer: 'The programme would probably have launched on time, but with a weaker process for complaints.' Modest, believable claims are more credible than dramatic ones. Panels can sense overclaiming.

The third is to be clear about measurement. If a programme reduced costs by a figure, say who calculated it and how. If the benefit was assessed independently, for example by internal audit or an external review, say so, as that supports your claim. If you do not have the number, explain what you do know, such as the direction of change and the evidence for it.

Remember that benefits of programmes are often realised later. State what had been achieved by the time you left or at the stage you describe, and what was still to come.

In probing, a panel may ask: 'What did others do that you did not?' or 'Where did you rely on others' judgement?' Answer generously. Recognising the contribution of colleagues is evidence of leadership, and it makes the account of your own part more believable.

Finally, ensure that your example is not stale. Recent evidence reassures the panel that you still operate at the level you describe.

questions.prompt: Which type of decision best evidences your own contribution to a large achievement?

options.text: A decision that was approved by a senior person after you had presented the options
A decision that was made by the whole group at a meeting, which you helped to prepare
A decision that followed the agreed plan and was delivered on time and to budget
One that would not have been taken in the same way without you

questions.prompt: Which counterfactual statement is most credible?

options.text: The programme would probably have launched on time but with a weaker complaints process
The programme would have been delayed by an unknown amount, since I cannot say how long
The programme would have been identical without me, since another colleague would have done the same
The programme would have failed without me, because I was the only person who understood the risk

questions.prompt: Why are dramatic claims about your contribution risky?

options.text: They are likely to be forgotten, as panels remember the more modest and measured claims
They are not allowed by the Code, which requires modesty in any account of your work
Panels can sense overclaiming and it reduces credibility
They take too long to explain, which leaves less time for the evidence the panel wants

questions.prompt: Which statement strengthens a claim about savings?

options.text: The saving was reported in the programme newsletter and shared across the department
The saving was larger than expected, which was noted by the programme board
The saving was calculated by the finance team and checked by internal audit
The saving was widely recognised in the department, including by senior colleagues

questions.prompt: You do not have an exact figure for the benefit. What should you say?

options.text: A rounded estimate that sounds plausible, so that the answer is complete and the panel can score it
That it is not relevant to your role, as you were responsible for delivery rather than benefits
What you know, such as the direction of change and the evidence for it
That the figure is confidential, so that you cannot be asked to give it in the interview

questions.prompt: Programme benefits were realised after you left. How should you present this?

options.text: Avoid mentioning it, since benefits that arrived after you left are not your evidence
Claim the full benefit as your own, since you set up the programme that delivered it
Say it was not your responsibility, so that the panel does not credit you with what others did
State what had been achieved by the time you left and what was still to come

questions.prompt: A panel asks, 'Where did you rely on others' judgement?' What is the best response?

options.text: Say you did not rely on anyone, because leaders are expected to make their own judgements
Say that it is not relevant, because the panel is scoring your own judgement and not theirs
Name specific areas and say why you trusted them, which shows generous leadership
Say that you relied on everyone equally, since the programme was a team effort throughout

questions.prompt: Why does recognising colleagues' contributions make your own account more believable?

options.text: It shows balanced judgement and that you are not claiming everything
It means you can claim less than you did, which protects you from being checked
It lets you skip the details of your own work and move on to the outcome
It reduces the panel's interest in your part, which lets you avoid detailed probing

questions.prompt: Why should the example be recent?

options.text: It reassures the panel that you still work at the level described
Older examples are less relevant to the Behaviour because the framework changes each year
Panels reject older examples outright, whatever the level of responsibility they describe
Recent examples are easier to remember, which makes it easier to answer probing questions

questions.prompt: Which question probes your individual contribution most directly?

options.text: How large was the team, and how many of them reported to you?
What did you do that others did not?
How did the programme end, and what happened to the people who worked on it?
How long did the programme last, and how long were you involved in it?

items.title: L14: Case studies with ethical and equality dimensions
items.source: Civil Service Code; Equality Act 2010; HM Treasury Green Book (GOV.UK)
items.body:
Senior case studies often contain a hidden ethical or legal issue. Three types recur.

The first is fairness between groups. An option might save money but disadvantage a group with a protected characteristic, such as disabled people or older people. The Public Sector Equality Duty requires public bodies to have due regard to the need to eliminate discrimination, advance equality of opportunity and foster good relations. In a case study, say that you would assess the impact on different groups, consult those affected and consider ways to reduce harm, rather than assume the decision is neutral.

The second is propriety and value for money. If a stakeholder presses for a particular supplier, or for spending that is not clearly justified, you should say that public money must be spent properly, fairly and with regard to value, and that you would follow procurement rules and seek advice from finance or commercial colleagues.

The third is honesty in evidence. A case study may include data that supports a conclusion a stakeholder wants. The right response is to use the evidence honestly, including parts that do not support the preferred conclusion, and say what the weaknesses are.

When you spot an issue, do not simply label it. Say what you would do: gather information, consult the right specialist, change the proposal or escalate. A candidate who says 'This raises equality issues' and moves on has scored less than one who explains how they would assess and manage them.

Proportionality matters too. Not every risk justifies a full process, but serious risks to individuals or to public trust do. State how you judge which is which.

Finally, be clear about your authority. You advise decision-makers, and where the decision is theirs, ensure they have what they need to make it lawfully and fairly.

questions.prompt: An option saves money but may disadvantage disabled people. What should a strong answer say?

options.text: The option should be rejected because it affects a group with a protected characteristic
The impact on different groups should be assessed, those affected consulted and ways to reduce harm considered
The saving is justified because public money is limited and the option meets the objective
The impact is a matter for the equalities team, not for the person making the decision

questions.hint: It meets the duty to have due regard.

questions.prompt: What does the Public Sector Equality Duty require of public bodies?

options.text: A report to Parliament on the equality impact of every decision that the body takes
Equal spending on each protected group so that no group receives more than another
Due regard to eliminating discrimination, advancing equality of opportunity and fostering good relations
A guarantee that no decision disadvantages any group with a protected characteristic

questions.hint: The duty is about due regard.

questions.prompt: A stakeholder presses for a particular supplier with no competition. What should you say?

options.text: Public money must be spent properly, fairly and with regard to value; you would follow procurement rules and seek commercial advice
The decision should be delayed until the next financial year, when new rules will apply
The supplier is probably the best option, so the rules can be applied flexibly this time
The stakeholder has the authority to choose, so the choice should be recorded and carried out

questions.prompt: A dataset supports the conclusion a stakeholder wants, but part of it does not. What should you do?

options.text: Use the supportive part only, since the stakeholder asked for evidence on that point
Ask for more data until it supports the conclusion, so that the recommendation is firm
Present the supportive part and mention the rest later, if the panel asks about it
Use all of the evidence honestly and state the weaknesses

questions.prompt: A candidate says 'This raises equality issues' and moves on. What is missing?

options.text: What they would do about it, such as assessing and managing the impact
A statement of the law that applies, so that the panel can see that the issue is understood
A mention of the Equality Act, which is the starting point for any discussion of the issue
A decision on the option, since naming the issue is enough once the choice has been made

questions.prompt: How should proportionality shape your response to risks in a case?

options.text: Only legal risks require action, as other risks are matters for the people who manage the work
Serious risks to individuals or public trust justify a fuller process, while minor ones do not
Every risk requires a full impact assessment, so that nothing is left to chance
Risks should be ranked by cost alone, since cost is the one measure that can be compared

questions.prompt: Who usually takes the decision in a case study in which you are an adviser?

options.text: The stakeholder who raised the issue, because they hold most of the information
The decision-maker, who must be given what they need to decide lawfully and fairly
The most senior person present, whatever their role in the decision process
You, as the adviser, since you have the best understanding of the evidence

questions.prompt: Why is it wise to consult those affected by a decision?

options.text: It transfers responsibility to those consulted, so that the decision-maker is protected
It is required for every decision, whatever its size or effect on the people involved
It improves the evidence and fairness, and may reduce harm
It slows the process so that fewer decisions are made in haste and later regretted

questions.prompt: Which action best handles pressure to overstate benefits?

options.text: Present the benefits as the stakeholder requests, since they know the context best
Refuse to continue with the exercise until the pressure has been withdrawn
Present the benefits honestly with the uncertainties
Leave out the benefits altogether so that nobody can say that they were overstated

questions.prompt: Which Civil Service Code value requires advice based on a fair assessment of the evidence?

options.text: Impartiality
Objectivity
Honesty
Integrity

items.title: L14: In-tray items for senior roles
items.source: Civil Service Code; ICO guidance on data breaches; Freedom of Information Act 2000 (GOV.UK)
items.body:
A senior in-tray exercise mixes operational crises with strategic decisions, and the main skill is knowing what only you can do and what to hand on.

Begin by scanning for anything that carries risk to people, the public or the department, such as a possible data breach, a safeguarding concern or a security issue. These come first and need action by the right people. The Information Commissioner's Office expects serious personal data breaches to be reported to it within 72 hours of the organisation becoming aware, so an in-tray that mentions a breach is likely to want you to alert the data protection officer immediately.

Next, consider items with fixed deadlines, such as a request from a minister's office with a specified time or a statutory time limit. Then consider the items that will matter most in the longer term, such as a team concern or a strategic decision. These need time, so protect it in the diary rather than letting urgent but less important items fill the day.

Delegate with clarity. Identify the right person, give them authority and context, set a time for reporting back and tell them what to escalate. Do not delegate a conversation that only you can have, such as a serious staff concern or a decision that carries your accountability.

A staff member raising a concern about wrongdoing should be taken seriously and handled under the department's procedures. Do not investigate it yourself or promise outcomes you cannot deliver.

Your replies should be brief and show why you made the choice. Also note what you decided not to do and why. Senior roles involve saying no.

questions.prompt: What should you scan for first in a senior in-tray?

options.text: Items that carry risk to people, the public or the department
Items from the most senior people, since their requests carry the greatest authority
Items with the shortest replies, so that you clear as many as possible before the time runs out
Items that can be done quickly, which gives you momentum for the harder ones

questions.prompt: Within what period should serious personal data breaches usually be reported to the ICO?

options.text: 72 hours of becoming aware
Ten working days, in line with the time given for responding to many information requests
One month after the breach, to allow for a proper investigation to be made first
24 hours of the breach occurring, whether or not the organisation knew about it

questions.prompt: The in-tray mentions a possible data breach. What is the best first action?

options.text: Investigate it yourself before telling anyone
Alert the data protection officer immediately
Wait for more information
Delegate to a junior colleague

questions.prompt: How should you handle important longer-term items such as a team concern?

options.text: Deal with them quickly in a single reply, so that they do not build up in the in-tray
Delegate them to a deputy, since a strategic decision can be taken at any level
Protect time in the diary so that urgent items do not crowd them out
Leave them until the urgent items are cleared, so that you can give them your full attention

questions.prompt: Which task should you not delegate?

options.text: A diary clash between two meetings that were accepted on your behalf
A serious staff concern conversation that only you can have
The booking of a meeting room for a team event later in the month
A routine reply to a supplier whose query is covered by the existing contract

questions.prompt: How should you delegate effectively?

options.text: Identify the right person, give authority and context, set a time to report back and say what to escalate
Tell them to come back to you if they need help, so that you are available but not intrusive
Send the task by email with a deadline, so that there is a written record of what was asked
Ask someone to take it over completely, so that you are not drawn back into the detail

questions.prompt: A staff member reports possible wrongdoing. What is the best response?

options.text: Take it seriously and handle it under the department's procedures, without investigating it yourself
Ask the person to raise it again in a week, so that you can see if the concern persists
Tell the staff member not to worry, since senior officials can judge what is serious
Investigate quickly yourself so that the issue is resolved before it spreads in the team

questions.prompt: Why should you note what you decided not to do?

options.text: To show the panel that you completed every item in the in-tray within the time
To reduce the length of the reply by listing the decisions in a single line
To keep a record for HR in case an item is later queried by a colleague
Senior roles involve saying no, and explaining it shows judgement

questions.prompt: Which item has a fixed deadline that sets its priority?

options.text: A routine update on a project that is not due for decision this quarter
An invitation to a long meeting next month that has been sent to all senior staff
A request for a development discussion from a member of your team
A request from a minister's office for an answer by a stated time

questions.prompt: What should replies in an in-tray exercise show?

options.text: A summary of your workload, so that the reader can see what else was competing for time
A detailed description of the item, so that the reader knows what you were responding to
A list of all the options that you considered, together with the costs of each of them
Brief reasoning for the choice made

items.title: L14: Questions about failures, accountability and reputation
items.source: Civil Service Code; Civil Service Success Profiles (GOV.UK)
items.body:
Senior panels often ask about things that went badly: a failed project, a service failure, an error that reached the press, or a team that missed its targets. They want to see accountability, learning and resilience. The way you speak about failure is itself evidence.

Accountability means owning what was in your control. If you were responsible for a team or a programme, say so, and avoid pointing at others or at circumstances. You can describe contributing factors, but start with your own part. A candidate who begins with 'The supplier let us down' appears to be shifting blame; one who begins 'I did not challenge the supplier's timetable early enough' appears accountable.

The next element is response. Describe what you did once you knew: how quickly you told the people who needed to know, how you protected those affected and how you stabilised the situation. In the Civil Service, early and honest escalation matters. Hiding or delaying bad news usually makes the consequences worse.

Learning comes last but is crucial. Explain what you changed, such as a new check, a different approach to supplier management or a clearer way of reporting risks, and whether it worked. A lesson that has led to action is stronger than a general reflection.

When a question concerns reputation, such as a complaint that attracted press attention, stay factual and balanced. Do not criticise colleagues or the department. Describe how you worked with the press office, supported the staff involved and used the incident to improve the service.

If you have not led a major failure, a smaller one is acceptable, as long as it is real. Do not invent a failure, and do not pick one so minor that it shows nothing. The panel is looking for self-awareness and growth.

questions.prompt: Which opening to a failure example shows the most accountability?

options.text: The department had not given us enough support, and I raised the point more than once
I did not challenge the supplier's timetable early enough
The timetable was unrealistic from the start, and I had said so when it was agreed
The supplier let us down, and the contract did not give us the powers that we needed

questions.prompt: What should be described after the failure became known?

options.text: How quickly you told those who needed to know, protected those affected and stabilised the situation
The causes of the failure in detail, so that the panel understands what went wrong
The reaction of the senior team, since their response shows how the failure was perceived
The cost of the failure to the department, and who agreed that the money could be spent

questions.prompt: Why is hiding or delaying bad news usually harmful?

options.text: It prevents learning
It makes the consequences worse and reduces trust
It is against the Civil Service Code in every case
It gives the press more time to investigate

questions.prompt: Which statement is the strongest evidence of learning?

options.text: I introduced a weekly supplier review and a risk report to the board, and delivery has since improved
I now know what to look out for, and I have shared that knowledge with colleagues
I would be more careful in future and I would check each stage of the plan more closely
I learned a great deal from the experience and it has changed how I approach my work

questions.prompt: How should you speak about colleagues involved in the failure?

options.text: By not mentioning them
With complaints about their role
By naming them
Factually and without criticism

questions.prompt: How should you answer when a question concerns a complaint that attracted press attention?

options.text: Say you cannot comment because the matter involved the press office, and move to the next question
Defend the department in strong terms, so that the panel sees your loyalty to the organisation
Stay factual and balanced and describe how you worked with the press office and supported staff
Explain how the press misreported the story, so that the facts are put right with the panel

questions.prompt: If you have not led a major failure, what is acceptable?

options.text: One that is invented so that you have a better story to tell the panel
One that is so minor it shows nothing about how you respond to difficulty
An example about someone else's failure that you watched and learned from at close range
A smaller but real one that shows what you learned

questions.prompt: What does a panel look for in failure answers?

options.text: Self-awareness, accountability and growth
A promise to avoid failure in future, which shows determination to improve
A confident defence of your decisions, to show that your judgement was sound at the time
A list of the external causes, so that the panel can see what was outside your control

questions.prompt: Which pair of elements should come first in a failure answer?

options.text: The cause and the cost, because they set the scale of the problem for the panel
The press coverage and the response, as this is the part that attracted most attention
The lessons and the outcome, since the panel wants to know what changed afterwards
Your own part and the facts of what happened

questions.prompt: Which answer would worry a panel most?

options.text: One that blames others and gives no learning
One that shows you escalated early and kept the people affected informed
One that is honest about a modest failure and explains what you changed afterwards
One that explains a mistake you made and what it cost the service

items.title: L14: Building a promotion strategy from feedback
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles and Civil Service Learning guidance (GOV.UK)
items.body:
Candidates who succeed at SEO level often treat promotion as a project that lasts a year or more. They collect feedback, build evidence, find advocates and choose the right moment. The approach has four parts.

First, diagnose. After each interview or assessment, record the feedback and look for patterns across several. Separate issues that can be fixed by practice, such as pace or structure, from issues of evidence, such as the lack of a leadership example at the right scale. The second group takes longer and needs planning.

Second, build evidence. Ask for assignments that stretch you towards the next grade: leading a cross-team workstream, representing the department at a senior meeting, managing a difficult stakeholder or covering for a manager. Temporary promotion or loan to another department can give broader experience. Keep records of what you do and the feedback you get, written soon after the event.

Third, find advocates. A mentor offers advice. A sponsor is someone senior who knows your work and will put your name forward. Be clear with your line manager about your ambition and ask them what they would need to see. Ask for feedback from people who have seen you perform at the next level, not only from those who have seen you in your current role.

Fourth, choose the moment. Apply when you can offer strong, recent examples at the level, not only because a vacancy exists. At the same time, avoid waiting for a perfect moment, as no candidate has perfect evidence. Where there is a reserve list, a strong performance may still lead to an offer.

Throughout, maintain performance in your current role. Promotion panels, referees and managers all look at how you are doing now.

questions.prompt: Which feedback issue takes longest to address?

options.text: Interview pace, which improves with repeated practice in front of other people
Use of filler words, which can be reduced by listening to a recording of your answers
Answer structure, which can be improved by planning each answer in advance
Lack of leadership evidence at the right scale

questions.prompt: Which assignment would best stretch you towards the next grade?

options.text: Taking on more of the same work you already do, so that you build up volume
Completing a training course on interview technique so that your answers improve
Moving to a team with fewer demands so that you have time to prepare for interviews
Leading a cross-team workstream or representing the department at a senior meeting

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a mentor and a sponsor?

options.text: A sponsor is paid by the department, while a mentor gives their time freely
A mentor is a friend outside work, and a sponsor is your line manager
They are the same role, and each word describes someone who gives feedback
A mentor offers advice; a sponsor is senior and puts your name forward

questions.prompt: Whose feedback is most valuable for evidence at the next level?

options.text: Your line manager only, since they are responsible for your appraisal
HR, who see the whole of your record and can give an objective view
People who have seen you perform at the next level
Your closest colleagues, who know your strengths and weaknesses in the greatest detail

questions.prompt: When is the right moment to apply?

options.text: Once a year, when the main promotion round takes place across the department
When you can offer strong, recent examples at the level
When your manager tells you to apply, since they know when you are ready
As soon as there is a vacancy, since the opportunity may not return for some time

questions.prompt: Why avoid waiting for the perfect moment?

options.text: Evidence is never perfect, and opportunities may not return
Vacancies are rare, so any delay reduces the number of chances that you have
Confidence matters more than evidence, so waiting for evidence is wasted time
Panels prefer candidates who apply often, as it shows determination

questions.prompt: Why keep records of what you do soon after the event?

options.text: Memory fades and records provide specific evidence
They are required by HR as part of the annual appraisal process
They help your manager to write a reference when you apply for promotion
They can be shown to the panel at interview as an addition to your answers

questions.prompt: Why maintain performance in your current role during a promotion push?

options.text: Your current role determines the grade for which you can apply, and performance sets it
You cannot be promoted if you leave your current role, as the grade depends on the post
HR checks your performance record and can stop the process if it has dipped
Panels, referees and managers all look at how you are doing now

questions.prompt: What can a reserve list mean for a candidate who was not appointed?

options.text: They must wait for six months before they are allowed to apply for another role
A strong performance may still lead to an offer later
They cannot reapply for the same role, since their application has already been considered
They will be appointed automatically when the next vacancy of that grade arises
